2: name: whole-project-protocol
3: description: >
4:   Mandatory whole-project planning, specification, implementation and verification
5:   protocol. Use it before and during any substantial project change. It prevents
6:   premature coding, incomplete implementations and false completion claims by
7:   maintaining a complete project model, finite executable TODO graph, acceptance
8:   criteria and verification evidence.
9: ---
10: 
11: # Whole Project Protocol
12: 
13: ## Purpose
14: 
15: Your responsibility is not merely to implement the user's latest request.
16: 
17: Your responsibility is to understand the project as a whole, determine what must exist for the requested outcome to be genuinely complete, implement that work, verify it, and maintain evidence showing why the project can be considered complete.
18: 
19: The fundamental rule is:
20: 
21: > NEVER CODE FROM A REQUEST ALONE.
22: > FIRST MODEL THE WHOLE CHANGE.
23: 
24: A project is complete only when the implementation, integrations, failure cases, tests, operational concerns, documentation, and acceptance criteria that are applicable to the requested scope have all been addressed.
25: 
26: ---
27: 
28: # 1. Core invariant
29: 
30: Every substantial change follows:
31: 
32: DISCOVER
33: → MODEL
34: → SPECIFY
35: → DECOMPOSE
36: → IMPLEMENT
37: → VERIFY
38: → CLOSE
39: 
40: Do not skip stages.
41: 
42: Do not silently merge stages.
43: 
44: Do not declare completion while verification work remains.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: # 2. Definition of "done"
49: 
50: "Done" NEVER means:
51: 
52: - code was written;
53: - the happy path works;
54: - tests written by the implementer pass;
55: - the requested UI is visible;
56: - the build succeeds;
57: - most TODOs are complete.
58: 
59: For this protocol:
60: 
61: DONE means all of the following are true:
62: 
63: 1. Requested behavior is implemented.
64: 2. Relevant existing behavior still works.
65: 3. Every applicable requirement has an acceptance criterion.
66: 4. Every acceptance criterion has verification evidence.
67: 5. All P0 and P1 TODOs are complete.
68: 6. No unclassified TODO remains.
69: 7. No critical or high unresolved defect remains.
70: 8. Required automated tests pass.
71: 9. Static checks pass when applicable.
72: 10. Build/package validation passes when applicable.
73: 11. Failure and recovery paths have been considered.
74: 12. Relevant security/privacy concerns have been considered.
75: 13. Relevant performance concerns have been considered.
76: 14. Relevant migration/backward compatibility concerns have been considered.
77: 15. Relevant observability/debuggability exists.
78: 16. Documentation reflects the resulting system.
79: 17. A final independent verification pass has been performed.
80: 18. A concise manual acceptance checklist has been produced for the user.
81: 
82: If any item is not applicable, explicitly mark it N/A and state why.
83: 
84: Never silently omit a category.
85: 
86: ---
87: 
88: # 3. Completion state machine
89: 
90: Use these exact conceptual states:
91: 
92: DISCOVERY
93: SPECIFICATION
94: PLANNED
95: IMPLEMENTING
96: VERIFYING
97: READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE
98: DONE
99: BLOCKED
100: 
101: The agent MUST NOT jump directly from IMPLEMENTING to DONE.
102: 
103: The normal final AI-controlled state is:
104: 
105: READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE
106: 
107: This means:
108: 
109: - all planned implementation is complete;
110: - automated verification is green;
111: - no known implementation work remains;
112: - the user may now perform final experiential/manual acceptance.
113: 
114: DONE may be used after manual acceptance when manual acceptance is required.
115: 
116: ---
117: 
118: # 4. Mandatory project artifacts
119: 
120: For substantial work, maintain a canonical project-completion directory.
121: 
122: Preferred location:
123: 
124: .agent/project/
125: 
126: Files:
127: 
128: 00-intent.md
129: 01-system-map.md
130: 02-spec.md
131: 03-acceptance.md
132: 04-work-graph.md
133: 05-risk-register.md
134: 06-verification-plan.md
135: 07-evidence.md
136: 08-manual-acceptance.md
137: 09-closure.md
138: state.json
139: 
140: Existing equivalent project documentation may be reused instead of duplicated.
141: 
142: The important requirement is semantic completeness, not the exact filenames.
143:

146: # 5. 00-intent.md
147: 
148: Capture the intended outcome.
149: 
150: Include:
151: 
152: ## Goal
153: 
154: What must be true for the user when this work is complete?
155: 
156: ## Non-goals
157: 
158: What is deliberately outside this scope?
159: 
160: ## User-visible outcome
161: 
162: Describe the final experience rather than implementation details.
163: 
164: ## Constraints
165: 
166: Technical, product, compatibility, platform, performance, security, UX or organizational constraints.
167: 
168: ## Completion sentence
169: 
170: Write one sentence:
171: 
172: "This project/change is complete when ..."
173: 
174: This sentence becomes the north star for the entire work graph.
175: 
176: ---
177: 
178: # 6. 01-system-map.md
179: 
180: Before coding, understand the surrounding system.
181: 
182: Map all relevant:
183: 
184: - entry points;
185: - modules;
186: - services;
187: - UI surfaces;
188: - state;
189: - persistence;
190: - schemas;
191: - APIs;
192: - external services;
193: - events;
194: - background jobs;
195: - permissions;
196: - authentication;
197: - configuration;
198: - deployment;
199: - tests;
200: - build pipelines;
201: - runtime dependencies;
202: - existing specifications;
203: - documentation.
204: 
205: Represent important flows end-to-end.
206: 
207: Example:
208: 
209: User Action
210: → View
211: → Application State
212: → Domain Logic
213: → Persistence
214: → Event
215: → Background Processing
216: → External Service
217: → Result
218: → UI Feedback
219: 
220: Do not treat a file as an isolated unit if the behavior crosses system boundaries.
221: 
222: ---

224: # 7. Repository discovery
225: 
226: Before planning implementation:
227: 
228: 1. Read project-level instructions.
229: 2. Read architecture documentation.
230: 3. Inspect relevant source code.
231: 4. Inspect existing tests.
232: 5. Inspect build and CI configuration.
233: 6. Inspect schemas/contracts.
234: 7. Search for related implementations.
235: 8. Identify conventions already used by the project.
236: 9. Identify known limitations.
237: 10. Check recent changes if relevant.
238: 
239: Never assume architecture from filenames alone.
240: 
241: When external APIs, frameworks, OS behavior or specifications affect correctness and uncertainty exists, consult authoritative external documentation before implementation.
242: 
243: ---

245: # 8. 02-spec.md
246: 
247: Produce the specification before implementation.
248: 
249: Every feature specification must cover where applicable:
250: 
251: ## Functional behavior
252: 
253: What the system must do.
254: 
255: ## User flows
256: 
257: Normal user journeys.
258: 
259: ## System flows
260: 
261: Internal behavior across components.
262: 
263: ## Data model
264: 
265: Inputs, outputs, schemas, persistence and ownership.
266: 
267: ## State transitions
268: 
269: Valid states and transitions.
270: 
271: ## Error behavior
272: 
273: Expected failures and how they surface.
274: 
275: ## Edge cases
276: 
277: Boundary conditions and unusual states.
278: 
279: ## Recovery
280: 
281: What happens after interruption, partial failure, restart or retry.
282: 
283: ## Concurrency
284: 
285: Race conditions, duplicate actions, idempotency and ordering where relevant.
286: 
287: ## Compatibility
288: 
289: Existing users, existing data, previous versions and integrations.
290: 
291: ## Security
292: 
293: Authentication, authorization, trust boundaries and abuse possibilities.
294: 
295: ## Privacy
296: 
297: Sensitive information, logging and retention where relevant.
298: 
299: ## Performance
300: 
301: Latency, memory, CPU, storage, networking and scaling concerns where relevant.
302: 
303: ## Accessibility
304: 
305: Keyboard interaction, screen readers, contrast, focus and motion where relevant.
306: 
307: ## Observability
308: 
309: How failures can later be diagnosed.
310: 
311: ## Deployment
312: 
313: Configuration, migrations, feature flags and rollback.
314:

317: # 9. Requirement IDs
318: 
319: Every requirement receives a stable identifier.
320: 
321: Examples:
322: 
323: REQ-001
324: REQ-002
325: REQ-003
326: 
327: Never create vague requirements such as:
328: 
329: "Make the screen work."
330: 
331: Prefer:
332: 
333: REQ-012:
334: When synchronization fails because connectivity disappears after the request starts,
335: the local document remains intact and the UI exposes a retry action without creating
336: duplicate remote records.
337: 
338: Requirements must be testable.
339:

342: # 10. 03-acceptance.md
343: 
344: Every requirement MUST map to one or more acceptance criteria.
345: 
346: Format:
347: 
348: AC-001
349: Requirement: REQ-001
350: 
351: Given:
352: ...
353: 
354: When:
355: ...
356: 
357: Then:
358: ...
359: 
360: Verification:
361: automated | inspection | runtime | manual
362: 
363: Evidence:

365: 
366: A requirement without acceptance criteria is incomplete.
367: 
368: An acceptance criterion without verification is incomplete.

429: # 12. 04-work-graph.md
430: 
431: Implementation must be represented as a finite work graph.
432: 
433: Each TODO contains:
434: 
435: ID
436: Priority
437: Status
438: Requirements
439: Dependencies
440: Description
441: Files/Systems
442: Acceptance Criteria
443: Verification Method
444: Evidence
445: Notes
446: 
447: Example:
448: 
449: TODO-P1-014
450: 
451: Priority: P1
452: Status: TODO
453: Requirements: REQ-012, REQ-013
454: Dependencies: TODO-P1-008
455:

463:

467: AC-024

477: # 13. TODO statuses
478: 
479: Only use:
480: 
481: TODO
482: READY
483: IN_PROGRESS
484: BLOCKED
485: VERIFYING
486: DONE
487: 
488: DONE requires evidence.
489: 
490: A TODO without evidence cannot be DONE.
491: 
492: ---
493: 
494: # 14. TODO priorities
495: 
496: P0:
497: The requested outcome fundamentally cannot work without this.
498: 
499: P1:
500: Required for a trustworthy complete implementation.
501: 
502: P2:
503: Useful improvement but may legitimately be deferred.
504: 
505: P3:
506: Optional idea.
507: 
508: Only P0 and P1 work defines project completion.
509: 
510: P2/P3 must never silently become part of the critical path.
511: 
512: Deferred work must remain explicitly documented.
513: 
514: ---
515: 
516: # 15. No coding before the planning gate
517: 
518: Implementation may begin only when:
519: 
520: - intent exists;
521: - relevant system map exists;
522: - specification exists;
523: - requirements are identified;
524: - acceptance criteria exist;
525: - work graph exists;
526: - critical unknowns are resolved;
527: - verification strategy exists.
528: 
529: For tiny or trivial changes these artifacts may be extremely short.
530: 
531: The protocol scales down.
532: 
533: It does not disappear.
534: 
535: ---
536: 
537: # 16. Planning completeness test
538: 
539: Before coding ask:
540: 
541: "If every TODO currently listed were completed perfectly, would the requested outcome actually be complete?"
542: 
543: If the answer may be no:
544: 
545: DO NOT START CODING.
546: 
547: Find the missing work.
548: 
549: Repeat until the answer is yes with reasonable confidence.
550: 
551: This question is one of the most important rules of the protocol.
552: 
553: ---
554: 
555: # 17. Implementation behavior
556: 
557: During implementation:
558: 
559: 1. Select a READY TODO.
560: 2. Mark it IN_PROGRESS.
561: 3. Implement only its intended scope.
562: 4. Run its local verification.
563: 5. Fix discovered regressions.
564: 6. Record evidence.
565: 7. Mark it DONE only after verification.
566: 8. Update the system/spec if implementation reveals incorrect assumptions.
567: 9. Recompute downstream TODOs if architecture changes.
568: 
569: The work graph is a living representation of reality.
570: 
571: Never keep a stale plan merely because it was written first.
572: 
573: ---
574: 
575: # 18. Discovered work rule
576: 
577: When implementation reveals additional necessary work:
578: 
579: DO NOT silently fix it.
580: 
581: Create a TODO.
582: 
583: Classify it.
584: 
585: Link it to its requirement/risk.
586: 
587: Then execute it according to priority.
588: 
589: This prevents invisible scope and forgotten work.
590: 
591: ---
592: 
593: # 19. Scope expansion rule
594: 
595: Do not treat every discovered improvement as mandatory.
596: 
597: Classify discovered items into:
598: 
599: REQUIRED_FOR_COMPLETION
600: DEFECT
601: TECHNICAL_DEBT
602: FOLLOW_UP
603: IDEA
604: 
605: Only the first two automatically enter the current P0/P1 completion path.
606: 
607: This prevents endless projects.
608: 
609: ---
610: 
611: # 20. Risk register
612: 
613: Maintain risks with:
614: 
615: ID
616: Description
617: Likelihood
618: Impact
619: Evidence
620: Mitigation
621: Status
622: 
623: Important categories:
624: 
625: - architectural assumptions;
626: - untested integration behavior;
627: - platform-specific behavior;
628: - third-party dependency behavior;
629: - data loss;
630: - migration failure;
631: - compatibility;
632: - concurrency;
633: - security;
634: - performance;
635: - missing observability.
636: 
637: No HIGH or CRITICAL unresolved risk may exist at closure.
638: 
639: ---
640: 
641: # 21. Verification architecture
642: 
643: Verification should be layered.
644: 
645: Prefer:
646: 
647: STATIC
648: → UNIT
649: → INTEGRATION
650: → SYSTEM
651: → E2E
652: → RUNTIME
653: → MANUAL
654: 
655: Not every project needs every layer.
656: 
657: But applicable layers must be explicitly classified.
658: 
659: ---
660: 
661: # 22. Verification independence
662: 
663: Whenever reasonably possible:
664: 
665: The agent performing final verification should not rely only on the reasoning of the implementation agent.
666: 
667: For multi-agent systems:
668: 
669: IMPLEMENTER AGENT
670: → produces implementation and evidence
671: 
672: VERIFIER AGENT
673: → independently reads the specification
674: → independently inspects the implementation
675: → executes verification
676: → attempts to falsify completion
677: → reports missing work
678: 
679: The verifier's task is not:
680: 
681: "Confirm this works."
682: 
683: The verifier's task is:
684: 
685: "Find evidence that this is not complete."
686: 
687: Only after failing to find such evidence should closure proceed.
688: 
689: ---
690: 
691: # 23. Adversarial verification
692: 
693: The final verification pass actively attempts:
694: 
695: - invalid inputs;
696: - missing inputs;
697: - repeated actions;
698: - interrupted operations;
699: - state corruption;
700: - stale state;
701: - restart/reload;
702: - partial completion;
703: - dependency failure;
704: - slow dependency;
705: - duplicated events;
706: - race conditions;
707: - permission denial;
708: - empty datasets;
709: - large datasets;
710: - upgrade paths;
711: - backward compatibility;
712: - unexpected navigation;
713: - user cancellation.
714: 
715: Only applicable cases need execution.
716: 
717: But they must be consciously considered.
718: 
719: ---
720: 
721: # 24. Regression requirement
722: 
723: A feature is not complete merely because the new behavior works.
724: 
725: The verifier must ask:
726: 
727: "What previously valid behavior could this change have broken?"
728: 
729: Relevant existing tests must run.
730: 
731: When test coverage is missing around an affected critical behavior, add appropriate coverage when practical.
732: 
733: ---
734: 
735: # 25. Evidence ledger
736: 
737: 07-evidence.md records proof.
738: 
739: Examples:
740: 
741: EV-001
742: AC: AC-022
743: Method: automated integration test
744: Command: ./scripts/test-sync.sh
745: Result: PASS
746: Timestamp: ...
747: Notes: retry generated one remote object and preserved local data.
748: 
749: EV-002
750: AC: AC-023
751: Method: code inspection
752: Result: PASS
753: Location: ...
754: Notes: idempotency key persisted before remote dispatch.
755: 
756: Never use:
757: 
758: "Looks correct."
759: 
760: as completion evidence.
761:

803: # 27. Completion audit
804: 
805: Before claiming completion, perform a complete audit.
806: 
807: Ask:
808: 
809: ## Specification
810: 
811: - Are all requirements still accurate?
812: - Did implementation introduce new behavior not represented in the spec?
813: 
814: ## TODOs
815: 
816: - Are all P0/P1 TODOs DONE?
817: - Are any hidden TODO comments, placeholders or temporary hacks left?
818: 
819: ## Acceptance
820: 
821: - Does every P0/P1 requirement have verified acceptance criteria?
822: 
823: ## Tests
824: 
825: - Are all relevant automated tests green?
826: - Were important regressions tested?
827: 
828: ## Runtime
829: 
830: - Was the real application exercised when possible?
831: 
832: ## Errors
833: 
834: - Were failure paths verified?
835: 
836: ## Data
837: 
838: - Is persistence/migration behavior verified?
839: 
840: ## Security
841: 
842: - Are relevant trust boundaries accounted for?
843: 
844: ## Performance
845: 
846: - Are known performance regressions absent?
847: 
848: ## Observability
849: 
850: - Could a failure be diagnosed?
851: 
852: ## Documentation
853: 
854: - Does documentation describe the system that now exists?
855: 
856: ## Repository
857: 
858: - No accidental files?
859: - No temporary debug behavior?
860: - No forgotten mock?
861: - No unexplained disabled test?
862: - No unresolved merge conflict?
863: - No relevant uncommitted generated artifact when repository policy requires it?
864: 
865: ## Risks
866: 
867: - No unresolved critical/high risk?
868: 
869: Any failing answer blocks closure.

875: The following phrases are prohibited while completion criteria remain unresolved:

878: "Finished"
879: "Complete"

881: "Everything works"
882: "Implementation complete"

956: # 30. Manual acceptance design
957: 
958: Manual acceptance is NOT the user's job of discovering basic implementation bugs.
959: 
960: Before presenting the manual checklist:
961: 
962: - automated checks should already be green;
963: - obvious runtime flows should already have been exercised where tooling permits;
964: - known bugs must already be documented;
965: - the agent must not knowingly hand broken software to the user.
966: 
967: The user's manual test should primarily answer:
968: 
969: "Does this feel and behave like the product I intended?"
970: 
971: not:
972: 
973: "Did the agent actually implement it?"
974: 
975: ---
976: 
977: # 31. User-reported failure after closure
978: 
979: If manual acceptance discovers a defect:
980: 
981: 1. Reopen the project.
982: 2. Set state to IMPLEMENTING.
983: 3. Create a defect requirement.
984: 4. Create acceptance criteria.
985: 5. Create a P0/P1 TODO.
986: 6. Add regression coverage.
987: 7. Fix.
988: 8. Re-run the whole relevant verification graph.
989: 9. Return to READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE.
990: 
991: Never patch outside the protocol.
992: 
993: ---
994: 
995: # 32. Multi-agent orchestration
996: 
997: For multi-agent systems there must be one canonical project state.
998: 
999: The orchestrator owns:
1000: 
1001: - global intent;
1002: - specification;
1003: - work graph;
1004: - dependency graph;
1005: - global state;
1006: - closure decision.
1007: 
1008: Sub-agents receive bounded work packets.
1009: 
1010: Every work packet contains:
1011: 
1012: TASK
1013: WHY
1014: REQUIREMENTS
1015: ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1016: ALLOWED SCOPE
1017: DEPENDENCIES
1018: VERIFICATION
1019: EXPECTED EVIDENCE
1020: 
1021: Sub-agents do not independently redefine project completion.
1022: 
1023: They report evidence back to the orchestrator.
1024:

# Whole Project Protocol

## Purpose

Your responsibility is not merely to implement the user's latest request.

Your responsibility is to understand the project as a whole, determine what must exist for the requested outcome to be genuinely complete, implement that work, verify it, and maintain evidence showing why the project can be considered complete.

The fundamental rule is:

> NEVER CODE FROM A REQUEST ALONE.
> FIRST MODEL THE WHOLE CHANGE.

A project is complete only when the implementation, integrations, failure cases, tests, operational concerns, documentation, and acceptance criteria that are applicable to the requested scope have all been addressed.

---

# 1. Core invariant

Every substantial change follows:

DISCOVER
→ MODEL
→ SPECIFY
→ DECOMPOSE
→ IMPLEMENT
→ VERIFY
→ CLOSE

Do not skip stages.

Do not silently merge stages.

Do not declare completion while verification work remains.

---

# 2. Definition of "done"

"Done" NEVER means:

- code was written;
- the happy path works;
- tests written by the implementer pass;
- the requested UI is visible;
- the build succeeds;
- most TODOs are complete.

For this protocol:

DONE means all of the following are true:

1. Requested behavior is implemented.
2. Relevant existing behavior still works.
3. Every applicable requirement has an acceptance criterion.
4. Every acceptance criterion has verification evidence.
5. All P0 and P1 TODOs are complete.
6. No unclassified TODO remains.
7. No critical or high unresolved defect remains.
8. Required automated tests pass.
9. Static checks pass when applicable.
10. Build/package validation passes when applicable.
11. Failure and recovery paths have been considered.
12. Relevant security/privacy concerns have been considered.
13. Relevant performance concerns have been considered.
14. Relevant migration/backward compatibility concerns have been considered.
15. Relevant observability/debuggability exists.
16. Documentation reflects the resulting system.
17. A final independent verification pass has been performed.
18. A concise manual acceptance checklist has been produced for the user.

If any item is not applicable, explicitly mark it N/A and state why.

Never silently omit a category.

---

# 3. Completion state machine

Use these exact conceptual states:

DISCOVERY
SPECIFICATION
PLANNED
IMPLEMENTING
VERIFYING
READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE
DONE
BLOCKED

The agent MUST NOT jump directly from IMPLEMENTING to DONE.

The normal final AI-controlled state is:

READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE

This means:

- all planned implementation is complete;
- automated verification is green;
- no known implementation work remains;
- the user may now perform final experiential/manual acceptance.

DONE may be used after manual acceptance when manual acceptance is required.

---

# 4. Mandatory project artifacts

For substantial work, maintain a canonical project-completion directory.

Preferred location:

.agent/project/

Files:

00-intent.md
01-system-map.md
02-spec.md
03-acceptance.md
04-work-graph.md
05-risk-register.md
06-verification-plan.md
07-evidence.md
08-manual-acceptance.md
09-closure.md
state.json

Existing equivalent project documentation may be reused instead of duplicated.

The important requirement is semantic completeness, not the exact filenames.

---

# 5. 00-intent.md

Capture the intended outcome.

Include:

## Goal

What must be true for the user when this work is complete?

## Non-goals

What is deliberately outside this scope?

## User-visible outcome

Describe the final experience rather than implementation details.

## Constraints

Technical, product, compatibility, platform, performance, security, UX or organizational constraints.

## Completion sentence

Write one sentence:

"This project/change is complete when ..."

This sentence becomes the north star for the entire work graph.

---

# 6. 01-system-map.md

Before coding, understand the surrounding system.

Map all relevant:

- entry points;
- modules;
- services;
- UI surfaces;
- state;
- persistence;
- schemas;
- APIs;
- external services;
- events;
- background jobs;
- permissions;
- authentication;
- configuration;
- deployment;
- tests;
- build pipelines;
- runtime dependencies;
- existing specifications;
- documentation.

Represent important flows end-to-end.

Example:

User Action
→ View
→ Application State
→ Domain Logic
→ Persistence
→ Event
→ Background Processing
→ External Service
→ Result
→ UI Feedback

Do not treat a file as an isolated unit if the behavior crosses system boundaries.

---

# 7. Repository discovery

Before planning implementation:

1. Read project-level instructions.
2. Read architecture documentation.
3. Inspect relevant source code.
4. Inspect existing tests.
5. Inspect build and CI configuration.
6. Inspect schemas/contracts.
7. Search for related implementations.
8. Identify conventions already used by the project.
9. Identify known limitations.
10. Check recent changes if relevant.

Never assume architecture from filenames alone.

When external APIs, frameworks, OS behavior or specifications affect correctness and uncertainty exists, consult authoritative external documentation before implementation.

---

# 8. 02-spec.md

Produce the specification before implementation.

Every feature specification must cover where applicable:

## Functional behavior

What the system must do.

## User flows

Normal user journeys.

## System flows

Internal behavior across components.

## Data model

Inputs, outputs, schemas, persistence and ownership.

## State transitions

Valid states and transitions.

## Error behavior

Expected failures and how they surface.

## Edge cases

Boundary conditions and unusual states.

## Recovery

What happens after interruption, partial failure, restart or retry.

## Concurrency

Race conditions, duplicate actions, idempotency and ordering where relevant.

## Compatibility

Existing users, existing data, previous versions and integrations.

## Security

Authentication, authorization, trust boundaries and abuse possibilities.

## Privacy

Sensitive information, logging and retention where relevant.

## Performance

Latency, memory, CPU, storage, networking and scaling concerns where relevant.

## Accessibility

Keyboard interaction, screen readers, contrast, focus and motion where relevant.

## Observability

How failures can later be diagnosed.

## Deployment

Configuration, migrations, feature flags and rollback.

---

# 9. Requirement IDs

Every requirement receives a stable identifier.

Examples:

REQ-001
REQ-002
REQ-003

Never create vague requirements such as:

"Make the screen work."

Prefer:

REQ-012:
When synchronization fails because connectivity disappears after the request starts,
the local document remains intact and the UI exposes a retry action without creating
duplicate remote records.

Requirements must be testable.

---

# 10. 03-acceptance.md

Every requirement MUST map to one or more acceptance criteria.

Format:

AC-001
Requirement: REQ-001

Given:
...

When:
...

Then:
...

Verification:
automated | inspection | runtime | manual

Evidence:
pending

A requirement without acceptance criteria is incomplete.

An acceptance criterion without verification is incomplete.

---

# 11. Whole-project coverage matrix

Before implementation, explicitly classify every category.

Use:

APPLICABLE
NOT APPLICABLE
UNKNOWN

Categories:

- core behavior
- UX
- loading states
- empty states
- error states
- cancellation
- retries
- persistence
- data integrity
- state restoration
- concurrency
- idempotency
- authentication
- authorization
- privacy
- security
- accessibility
- performance
- networking
- offline behavior
- caching
- migrations
- backward compatibility
- API contracts
- external integrations
- logging
- metrics
- diagnostics
- testability
- unit tests
- integration tests
- end-to-end tests
- build
- packaging
- deployment
- rollback
- documentation
- developer experience
- user migration
- cleanup of obsolete behavior

UNKNOWN categories must be resolved before closure.

---

# 12. 04-work-graph.md

Implementation must be represented as a finite work graph.

Each TODO contains:

ID
Priority
Status
Requirements
Dependencies
Description
Files/Systems
Acceptance Criteria
Verification Method
Evidence
Notes

Example:

TODO-P1-014

Priority: P1
Status: TODO
Requirements: REQ-012, REQ-013
Dependencies: TODO-P1-008

Description:
Implement retry-safe persistence for interrupted synchronization.

Affected:
SyncCoordinator
DocumentStore
SyncIntegrationTests

Acceptance:
AC-022
AC-023
AC-024

Verification:
./scripts/test-sync.sh

Evidence:
pending

---

# 13. TODO statuses

Only use:

TODO
READY
IN_PROGRESS
BLOCKED
VERIFYING
DONE

DONE requires evidence.

A TODO without evidence cannot be DONE.

---

# 14. TODO priorities

P0:
The requested outcome fundamentally cannot work without this.

P1:
Required for a trustworthy complete implementation.

P2:
Useful improvement but may legitimately be deferred.

P3:
Optional idea.

Only P0 and P1 work defines project completion.

P2/P3 must never silently become part of the critical path.

Deferred work must remain explicitly documented.

---

# 15. No coding before the planning gate

Implementation may begin only when:

- intent exists;
- relevant system map exists;
- specification exists;
- requirements are identified;
- acceptance criteria exist;
- work graph exists;
- critical unknowns are resolved;
- verification strategy exists.

For tiny or trivial changes these artifacts may be extremely short.

The protocol scales down.

It does not disappear.

---

# 16. Planning completeness test

Before coding ask:

"If every TODO currently listed were completed perfectly, would the requested outcome actually be complete?"

If the answer may be no:

DO NOT START CODING.

Find the missing work.

Repeat until the answer is yes with reasonable confidence.

This question is one of the most important rules of the protocol.

---

# 17. Implementation behavior

During implementation:

1. Select a READY TODO.
2. Mark it IN_PROGRESS.
3. Implement only its intended scope.
4. Run its local verification.
5. Fix discovered regressions.
6. Record evidence.
7. Mark it DONE only after verification.
8. Update the system/spec if implementation reveals incorrect assumptions.
9. Recompute downstream TODOs if architecture changes.

The work graph is a living representation of reality.

Never keep a stale plan merely because it was written first.

---

# 18. Discovered work rule

When implementation reveals additional necessary work:

DO NOT silently fix it.

Create a TODO.

Classify it.

Link it to its requirement/risk.

Then execute it according to priority.

This prevents invisible scope and forgotten work.

---

# 19. Scope expansion rule

Do not treat every discovered improvement as mandatory.

Classify discovered items into:

REQUIRED_FOR_COMPLETION
DEFECT
TECHNICAL_DEBT
FOLLOW_UP
IDEA

Only the first two automatically enter the current P0/P1 completion path.

This prevents endless projects.

---

# 20. Risk register

Maintain risks with:

ID
Description
Likelihood
Impact
Evidence
Mitigation
Status

Important categories:

- architectural assumptions;
- untested integration behavior;
- platform-specific behavior;
- third-party dependency behavior;
- data loss;
- migration failure;
- compatibility;
- concurrency;
- security;
- performance;
- missing observability.

No HIGH or CRITICAL unresolved risk may exist at closure.

---

# 21. Verification architecture

Verification should be layered.

Prefer:

STATIC
→ UNIT
→ INTEGRATION
→ SYSTEM
→ E2E
→ RUNTIME
→ MANUAL

Not every project needs every layer.

But applicable layers must be explicitly classified.

---

# 22. Verification independence

Whenever reasonably possible:

The agent performing final verification should not rely only on the reasoning of the implementation agent.

For multi-agent systems:

IMPLEMENTER AGENT
→ produces implementation and evidence

VERIFIER AGENT
→ independently reads the specification
→ independently inspects the implementation
→ executes verification
→ attempts to falsify completion
→ reports missing work

The verifier's task is not:

"Confirm this works."

The verifier's task is:

"Find evidence that this is not complete."

Only after failing to find such evidence should closure proceed.

---

# 23. Adversarial verification

The final verification pass actively attempts:

- invalid inputs;
- missing inputs;
- repeated actions;
- interrupted operations;
- state corruption;
- stale state;
- restart/reload;
- partial completion;
- dependency failure;
- slow dependency;
- duplicated events;
- race conditions;
- permission denial;
- empty datasets;
- large datasets;
- upgrade paths;
- backward compatibility;
- unexpected navigation;
- user cancellation.

Only applicable cases need execution.

But they must be consciously considered.

---

# 24. Regression requirement

A feature is not complete merely because the new behavior works.

The verifier must ask:

"What previously valid behavior could this change have broken?"

Relevant existing tests must run.

When test coverage is missing around an affected critical behavior, add appropriate coverage when practical.

---

# 25. Evidence ledger

07-evidence.md records proof.

Examples:

EV-001
AC: AC-022
Method: automated integration test
Command: ./scripts/test-sync.sh
Result: PASS
Timestamp: ...
Notes: retry generated one remote object and preserved local data.

EV-002
AC: AC-023
Method: code inspection
Result: PASS
Location: ...
Notes: idempotency key persisted before remote dispatch.

Never use:

"Looks correct."

as completion evidence.

---

# 26. Machine-readable state

Maintain `state.json`.

Example conceptual schema:

{
  "phase": "VERIFYING",
  "requirements": {
    "total": 24,
    "covered": 24
  },
  "todos": {
    "p0_open": 0,
    "p1_open": 0,
    "p2_open": 3
  },
  "acceptance": {
    "total": 31,
    "verified": 29,
    "failed": 0,
    "pending": 2
  },
  "risks": {
    "critical_open": 0,
    "high_open": 0
  },
  "verification": {
    "status": "running"
  },
  "ready_for_manual_acceptance": false
}

The exact schema may evolve.

The state MUST reflect reality.

---

# 27. Completion audit

Before claiming completion, perform a complete audit.

Ask:

## Specification

- Are all requirements still accurate?
- Did implementation introduce new behavior not represented in the spec?

## TODOs

- Are all P0/P1 TODOs DONE?
- Are any hidden TODO comments, placeholders or temporary hacks left?

## Acceptance

- Does every P0/P1 requirement have verified acceptance criteria?

## Tests

- Are all relevant automated tests green?
- Were important regressions tested?

## Runtime

- Was the real application exercised when possible?

## Errors

- Were failure paths verified?

## Data

- Is persistence/migration behavior verified?

## Security

- Are relevant trust boundaries accounted for?

## Performance

- Are known performance regressions absent?

## Observability

- Could a failure be diagnosed?

## Documentation

- Does documentation describe the system that now exists?

## Repository

- No accidental files?
- No temporary debug behavior?
- No forgotten mock?
- No unexplained disabled test?
- No unresolved merge conflict?
- No relevant uncommitted generated artifact when repository policy requires it?

## Risks

- No unresolved critical/high risk?

Any failing answer blocks closure.

---

# 28. False-completion guard

The following phrases are prohibited while completion criteria remain unresolved:

"Done"
"Finished"
"Complete"
"Ready"
"Everything works"
"Implementation complete"

Instead report:

"Implementation is progressing. Remaining completion blockers: ..."

---

# 29. Closure output

Once all automated and agent-controlled completion requirements pass, the final report must use:

# READY FOR MANUAL ACCEPTANCE

## Outcome

One short description of what now exists.

## Completion

P0 remaining: 0
P1 remaining: 0
Acceptance criteria pending: 0
Failed acceptance criteria: 0
Critical risks: 0
High risks: 0

## Verification performed

List the important verification commands/checks and results.

## Evidence

Reference relevant evidence IDs.

## Deferred non-blocking work

List P2/P3 items only.

If none:

None.

## Known limitations

State real limitations.

If none are currently known:

No known blocking limitations.

Never claim that unknown bugs cannot exist.

## Manual acceptance

Provide the shortest useful manual checklist allowing the user to experience the completed result.

Example:

1. Launch the application.
2. Create a new document.
3. Perform X.
4. Confirm Y.
5. Restart the application.
6. Confirm the result persists.

## Final status

READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE

The project contains no known remaining P0/P1 implementation work.

---

# 30. Manual acceptance design

Manual acceptance is NOT the user's job of discovering basic implementation bugs.

Before presenting the manual checklist:

- automated checks should already be green;
- obvious runtime flows should already have been exercised where tooling permits;
- known bugs must already be documented;
- the agent must not knowingly hand broken software to the user.

The user's manual test should primarily answer:

"Does this feel and behave like the product I intended?"

not:

"Did the agent actually implement it?"

---

# 31. User-reported failure after closure

If manual acceptance discovers a defect:

1. Reopen the project.
2. Set state to IMPLEMENTING.
3. Create a defect requirement.
4. Create acceptance criteria.
5. Create a P0/P1 TODO.
6. Add regression coverage.
7. Fix.
8. Re-run the whole relevant verification graph.
9. Return to READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE.

Never patch outside the protocol.

---

For multi-agent systems there must be one canonical project state.

The orchestrator owns:

- global intent;
- specification;
- work graph;
- dependency graph;
- global state;
- closure decision.

VERIFICATION
EXPECTED EVIDENCE

Sub-agents do not independently redefine project completion.

They report evidence back to the orchestrator.

Only the orchestrator may transition the overall project to:

READY_FOR_MANUAL_ACCEPTANCE.

1: /**
2:  * Core: the event store, and the session it makes possible.
3:  *
4:  * This is the primitive the whole project rests on, and the reason it exists at
5:  * all. A conversation is a rendering of a state, not the state itself: today an
6:  * agent session dies with its process, and everything it learned dies with it.
7:  * Here, an append-only log of events is the state. The transcript, the
8:  * transcript of the language model included, is a projection that can be
9:  * rebuilt and thrown away.
10:  *
11:  * The design commitment that follows from that: the log is append-only and the
12:  * store performs no I/O, exactly like the ownership and capability cores. A
13:  * caller supplies the event list, the store folds it into a Session, and the
14:  * caller persists it however it likes. That keeps the whole thing testable
15:  * without a machine and without a clock, and it means the storage engine is an
16:  * adapter matter, decided later on evidence rather than now.
17:  *
18:  * It is called an event store and not a database on purpose. SQLite arrives
19:  * when a replay measurement justifies it, and not before.
20:  */
21: 
22: /** Something that happened, once, and can never be contradicted. */
23: export interface Event {
24:   /** Monotonic within a session, assigned by appendEvent, stable forever. */
25:   seq: number;
26:   /** Wall clock at append time. Injected, never read from Date inside. */
27:   at: number;
28:   /**
29:    * What kind of thing happened. A closed vocabulary, because every consumer
30:    * switches on it: goal, capability, directive, observation, action, evidence,
31:    * model, note.
32:    */
33:   kind: EventKind;
34:   /** The subject the event is about, e.g. an agent id or a capability name. */
35:   subject: string;
36:   /** Facts carried by the event. Shape is per-kind, and the core ignores it. */
37:   data: Record<string, unknown>;
38: }
39: 
40: export type EventKind =
41:   | "goal"
42:   | "capability"
43:   | "directive"
44:   | "observation"
45:   | "action"
46:   | "evidence"
47:   | "model"
48:   | "note"
49:   | // An effect the world was asked to perform. Recording the request is not
50:     // recording its outcome, and the two must never be the same fact: the whole
51:     // point of an id here is that a request can be observed, or never observed,
52:     // and those are three states rather than two.
53:     "effect_requested"
54:   | // What the world answered about one effect. Carries the id of the request
55:     // it answers, so a crash between the two leaves an unanswered request
56:     // rather than a guess.
57:     "effect_observed"
58:   | // That a worker asserted it produced something. An assertion, not a
59:     // satisfaction: the artifact is named and nobody has checked it yet.
60:     "work_produced"
61:   | // What an independent check concluded about a named artifact. Its own kind
62:     // rather than a field on the production event, so that a rejection is a
63:     // second historical fact and the first one survives. VER-04.
64:     "work_verified";
65: 
66: /**
67:  * Every kind, as a value.
68:  *
69:  * The union above is what a consumer switches on. This is the same list as a
70:  * value, so a projection or a validator can enumerate it without restating it
71:  * and drifting from the definition.
72:  */
73: export const EVENT_KINDS_OF_STORE = [
74:   "goal",
75:   "capability",
76:   "directive",
77:   "observation",
78:   "action",
79:   "evidence",
80:   "model",
81:   "note",

83:   "effect_observed",
84:   "work_produced",
85:   "work_verified",

90: 
91: /** A goal, as reconstructed from the events that mention it. */
92: export interface Goal {
93:   subject: string;
94:   text: string;
95:   at: number;
96:   /** False once a later event of kind evidence closes it. */

98: }

101: export interface Directive {

103:   at: number;
104:   target: string;
105:   text: string;

145: export class EventStore {
146:   readonly id: string;
147:   private readonly now: () => number;
148:   private readonly events: Event[] = [];
149:   private nextSeq = 1;
150: 
151:   // Parameter properties are avoided on purpose: this project runs under
152:   // Node's strip-only TypeScript mode, which does not support them, and the
153:   // rest of the core writes fields explicitly for the same reason.
154:   constructor(id: string, now: () => number) {
155:     this.id = id;
156:     this.now = now;
157:   }
158: 
159:   /**
160:    * Append one event. A caller supplies `at` when replaying historical data and
161:    * omits it when recording live, so that a replay is bit-identical to the
162:    * original. Events are never mutated and never removed; a mistake is
163:    * corrected by appending an event that says so.
164:    */
165:   append(event: NewEvent): Event {
166:     const stamped: Event = {
167:       ...event,
168:       seq: this.nextSeq++,
169:       at: event.at ?? this.now(),
170:     };
171:     this.events.push(stamped);
172:     return stamped;
173:   }

175:   /**
176:    * The revision this store is at: the sequence of the last event appended.
177:    *
178:    * A number, not a hash. The journal is already sequenced, so "is what I read
179:    * still current" is a comparison, not a recomputation. A state hash would
180:    * detect a change this revision detects, and would also cost a pass over the
181:    * whole log to detect nothing, so there is no reason to have one until a
182:    * case appears that sequence cannot express.
183:    */
184:   get revision(): number {
185:     // -1 rather than 0 for the empty journal, and it has to match the fold:
186:     // sequence 1 is the first event, so "the last event there is" is undefined
187:     // rather than zero. Returning 0 would let a caller that read nothing claim
188:     // to have read revision 0, which nothing ever occupies.
189:     return this.events.length === 0 ? -1 : this.events[this.events.length - 1]!.seq;

194:    *
195:    * This is the whole of P10. A surface derives an affordance from the state it

197:    * appended. Both decisions were locally valid against what each had seen, and
198:    * the second one would be wrong by the time it lands. That is TOCTOU, and it
199:    * is fixed by making the check and the append one operation rather than two.
200:    *
201:    * `expectedRevision` is the revision the caller's affordance was derived

207:    * was written, which is CON-03.
208:    */

210:     if (this.revision !== expectedRevision) return null;
211:     return this.append(event);

218:    * are read, because a projection only ever moves forward.

/**
 * Core: the event store, and the session it makes possible.
 *
 * This is the primitive the whole project rests on, and the reason it exists at
 * all. A conversation is a rendering of a state, not the state itself: today an
 * agent session dies with its process, and everything it learned dies with it.
 * Here, an append-only log of events is the state. The transcript, the
 * transcript of the language model included, is a projection that can be
 * rebuilt and thrown away.
 *
 * The design commitment that follows from that: the log is append-only and the
 * store performs no I/O, exactly like the ownership and capability cores. A
 * caller supplies the event list, the store folds it into a Session, and the
 * caller persists it however it likes. That keeps the whole thing testable
 * without a machine and without a clock, and it means the storage engine is an
 * adapter matter, decided later on evidence rather than now.
 *
 * It is called an event store and not a database on purpose. SQLite arrives
 * when a replay measurement justifies it, and not before.

36: 
37: ## Une logique commune, plusieurs projections
38: 
39: Flux recommandé :
40: 
41: ```text
42: intention + révision
43:   -> travail identifié
44:   -> demande d'aide typée
45:   -> admission et choix du destinataire / modèle
46:   -> exécution isolée
47:   -> résultat et références de preuves
48:   -> publication centrale qualifiée
49:   -> deltas pertinents aux agents et à la vue humaine
50: ```
51: 
52: Le contrôleur écrit un événement durable avant de publier sa notification.
53: L'enveloppe minimale relie `eventId`, `requestId`, `causationId`, `agentId`,
54: `taskId`, `objectiveRevision`, `scope`, `sourceRefs` et `schemaVersion`.
55: Un curseur par consommateur permet la reprise et la déduplication. La vue ne
56: conclut pas qu'une tâche est terminée parce qu'un flux a fermé.
57: 
58: | Objet central proposé | Ce que l'agent reçoit | Ce que l'humain voit |
59: |---|---|---|
60: | Demande d'aide | Question, résultat attendu, limites, sources accessibles | Qui aide qui, pour débloquer quoi |
61: | Décision de route | Route choisie, contraintes, motif et candidats exclus | Modèle effectif et raison courte, détail à la demande |
62: | Résultat d'aide | Constat qualifié, implications, inconnues et sources | Découverte qui change le travail, source ouvrable |
63: | Delta de connaissance | Changement pertinent, révision et invalidateurs | Ce qui vient de changer dans la compréhension commune |
64: | Reçu de validation | Critère vérifié, commande ou méthode, cible et révision | Ce qui est démontré et ce qui reste à vérifier |
65: 
66: Ce sont des projections des mêmes identités. Leur contenu est filtré selon les
67: droits et le besoin. Une vue d'inspection peut exposer plus de détail sans créer
68: une seconde mémoire. Les tokens de texte en cours peuvent rester éphémères ;
69: les décisions, résultats, effets et preuves nécessaires à la reprise sont durables.
70: 
71: ## Routage : commencer avec des règles vérifiables
72: 
73: Proposition pour AR03/AR04 :
74: 
75: 1. Filtrer les routes par autorisation, données accessibles, format, outils,
76:    contexte requis et contraintes humaines. Inconnu reste explicite.
77: 2. Appliquer l'état récent de disponibilité au niveau route/déploiement et la
78:    pression collective du fournisseur. Un quota refusé ne devient pas un mauvais
79:    score de compétence au code.
80: 3. Honorer un choix humain applicable ; sinon démarrer avec le défaut configuré
81:    et les préférences explicites. Tout changement a un motif consultable.
82: 4. Utiliser les résultats vérifiés de tâches comparables, leur fraîcheur et leur
83:    nombre d'observations. Ne pas prétendre à une estimation fiable avec un seul essai.
84: 5. Escalader après une cause identifiée, dans le budget commun. Reconstituer une
85:    capsule depuis l'état durable ; ne jamais rejouer automatiquement un effet incertain.
86: 
87: Enregistrer séparément : transport, quota/auth, format de réponse, validité
88: d'appel d'outil, exécution, puis satisfaction du critère. Un outil échoué peut
89: révéler un dépôt défectueux ou un contrat ambigu, pas une faiblesse du modèle.
90: Mesurer le temps jusqu'à un résultat vérifié et le coût total des reprises,
91: plutôt que la seule latence du premier token.
92: 
93: ## Entraide universelle sans boucle incontrôlée
94: 
95: Tous les rôles appellent le même service `requestAssistance`. Le service cherche
96: un résultat frais réutilisable, puis un pair pertinent, puis admet un helper si
97: nécessaire. Chaque demande porte une échéance et une réserve du budget global.
98: Le rôle du demandeur ne lui donne pas de nouvelles permissions.
99: 
100: La file d'attente doit détecter les dépendances cycliques et libérer le slot de
101: calcul d'un agent qui attend. Une demande équivalente peut partager le même travail
102: d'aide si scopes, sources et révision correspondent. Une annulation ferme les
103: nouvelles admissions mais conserve les résultats déjà confirmés.
104: 
105: Pour nourrir le cœur, publier une connaissance avec auteur, sources, révision,
106: statut OBSERVED/INFERRED/ASSUMED/UNKNOWN et invalidateurs. Un avis reçu reste
107: INFERRED même si trois agents l'approuvent. Sa validation ajoute un reçu séparé.
108: Les découvertes périmées restent consultables historiquement mais cessent de
109: justifier les actions courantes. L'accès à un résumé ne doit jamais donner accès
110: implicitement à ses sources privées.
111: 
112: ## Vérifications qui peuvent contredire la proposition
113: 
114: - Fermer puis rouvrir la vue pendant une aide : même demande, aucune nouvelle
115:   inférence déclenchée par le simple affichage.
116: - Corriger l'intention entre résultat et effet : résultat marqué périmé, aucune
117:   application sous l'ancienne révision.
118: - Recevoir deux fois un résultat : une seule publication et une seule dépense
119:   admise pour la demande coalescée, sans promettre l'exactly-once du fournisseur.
120: - A attend B qui attend A : cycle visible, budget conservé, terminal utilisable.
121: - Fournisseur refuse tous les agents : backpressure commune, aucune tempête
122:   de retries, brouillon et preuves conservés.
123: - Helper affirme que le code marche : statut d'avis reçu seulement ; les critères
124:   restent ouverts jusqu'à leurs validations.
125: - Redémarrer pendant un effet : reçu retrouvé ou effet incertain, jamais succès
126:   déduit de l'absence d'erreur.
127: 
128: Ces scénarios sont un plan proposé, pas des tests exécutés dans cette recherche.
129: Le parcours réel final doit relier demande d'aide, route choisie, découverte
130: centrale, consommation par un autre agent et preuve visible après redémarrage.
131: 
132: ## Ce que cette recherche ne justifie pas
133: 
134: Pas de réécriture en Rust, de migration LangGraph, de service LiteLLM obligatoire,
135: de bus distribué ni d'intégration A2A réseau dans la première tranche. Ces outils
136: peuvent devenir des adaptateurs si un besoin mesuré les justifie. Le travail
137: prioritaire consiste à relier les mécanismes Cuesheet existants sous un contrat
138: commun et à démontrer leur continuité dans le vrai terminal.
139: 
140: Vérification documentaire : huit sources primaires ouvertes ; faits externes
141: séparés des recommandations ; aucune annonce d'implémentation ; liens entre

143: incertains, mélange de scopes, cycles, budgets et attribution trompeuse des
144: résultats au modèle. Aucun test runtime ni build requis pour ce seul document.

## Une logique commune, plusieurs projections

Flux recommandé :

```text
intention + révision
  -> travail identifié
  -> demande d'aide typée
  -> admission et choix du destinataire / modèle
  -> exécution isolée
  -> résultat et références de preuves
  -> publication centrale qualifiée
  -> deltas pertinents aux agents et à la vue humaine
```

Le contrôleur écrit un événement durable avant de publier sa notification.
L'enveloppe minimale relie `eventId`, `requestId`, `causationId`, `agentId`,
`taskId`, `objectiveRevision`, `scope`, `sourceRefs` et `schemaVersion`.
Un curseur par consommateur permet la reprise et la déduplication. La vue ne
conclut pas qu'une tâche est terminée parce qu'un flux a fermé.

| Objet central proposé | Ce que l'agent reçoit | Ce que l'humain voit |
|---|---|---|
| Demande d'aide | Question, résultat attendu, limites, sources accessibles | Qui aide qui, pour débloquer quoi |
| Décision de route | Route choisie, contraintes, motif et candidats exclus | Modèle effectif et raison courte, détail à la demande |
| Résultat d'aide | Constat qualifié, implications, inconnues et sources | Découverte qui change le travail, source ouvrable |
| Delta de connaissance | Changement pertinent, révision et invalidateurs | Ce qui vient de changer dans la compréhension commune |
| Reçu de validation | Critère vérifié, commande ou méthode, cible et révision | Ce qui est démontré et ce qui reste à vérifier |

Ce sont des projections des mêmes identités. Leur contenu est filtré selon les
droits et le besoin. Une vue d'inspection peut exposer plus de détail sans créer
une seconde mémoire. Les tokens de texte en cours peuvent rester éphémères ;
les décisions, résultats, effets et preuves nécessaires à la reprise sont durables.

## Routage : commencer avec des règles vérifiables

Proposition pour AR03/AR04 :

1. Filtrer les routes par autorisation, données accessibles, format, outils,
   contexte requis et contraintes humaines. Inconnu reste explicite.
2. Appliquer l'état récent de disponibilité au niveau route/déploiement et la
   pression collective du fournisseur. Un quota refusé ne devient pas un mauvais
   score de compétence au code.
3. Honorer un choix humain applicable ; sinon démarrer avec le défaut configuré
   et les préférences explicites. Tout changement a un motif consultable.
4. Utiliser les résultats vérifiés de tâches comparables, leur fraîcheur et leur
   nombre d'observations. Ne pas prétendre à une estimation fiable avec un seul essai.
5. Escalader après une cause identifiée, dans le budget commun. Reconstituer une
   capsule depuis l'état durable ; ne jamais rejouer automatiquement un effet incertain.

Enregistrer séparément : transport, quota/auth, format de réponse, validité
d'appel d'outil, exécution, puis satisfaction du critère. Un outil échoué peut
révéler un dépôt défectueux ou un contrat ambigu, pas une faiblesse du modèle.
Mesurer le temps jusqu'à un résultat vérifié et le coût total des reprises,
plutôt que la seule latence du premier token.

## Entraide universelle sans boucle incontrôlée

Tous les rôles appellent le même service `requestAssistance`. Le service cherche
un résultat frais réutilisable, puis un pair pertinent, puis admet un helper si
nécessaire. Chaque demande porte une échéance et une réserve du budget global.
Le rôle du demandeur ne lui donne pas de nouvelles permissions.

La file d'attente doit détecter les dépendances cycliques et libérer le slot de
calcul d'un agent qui attend. Une demande équivalente peut partager le même travail
d'aide si scopes, sources et révision correspondent. Une annulation ferme les
nouvelles admissions mais conserve les résultats déjà confirmés.

Pour nourrir le cœur, publier une connaissance avec auteur, sources, révision,
statut OBSERVED/INFERRED/ASSUMED/UNKNOWN et invalidateurs. Un avis reçu reste
INFERRED même si trois agents l'approuvent. Sa validation ajoute un reçu séparé.
Les découvertes périmées restent consultables historiquement mais cessent de
justifier les actions courantes. L'accès à un résumé ne doit jamais donner accès
implicitement à ses sources privées.

## Vérifications qui peuvent contredire la proposition

- Fermer puis rouvrir la vue pendant une aide : même demande, aucune nouvelle
  inférence déclenchée par le simple affichage.
- Corriger l'intention entre résultat et effet : résultat marqué périmé, aucune
  application sous l'ancienne révision.
- Recevoir deux fois un résultat : une seule publication et une seule dépense
  admise pour la demande coalescée, sans promettre l'exactly-once du fournisseur.
- A attend B qui attend A : cycle visible, budget conservé, terminal utilisable.
- Fournisseur refuse tous les agents : backpressure commune, aucune tempête
  de retries, brouillon et preuves conservés.
- Helper affirme que le code marche : statut d'avis reçu seulement ; les critères
  restent ouverts jusqu'à leurs validations.
- Redémarrer pendant un effet : reçu retrouvé ou effet incertain, jamais succès
  déduit de l'absence d'erreur.

Ces scénarios sont un plan proposé, pas des tests exécutés dans cette recherche.
Le parcours réel final doit relier demande d'aide, route choisie, découverte
centrale, consommation par un autre agent et preuve visible après redémarrage.

## Ce que cette recherche ne justifie pas

Pas de réécriture en Rust, de migration LangGraph, de service LiteLLM obligatoire,
de bus distribué ni d'intégration A2A réseau dans la première tranche. Ces outils
peuvent devenir des adaptateurs si un besoin mesuré les justifie. Le travail
prioritaire consiste à relier les mécanismes Cuesheet existants sous un contrat
commun et à démontrer leur continuité dans le vrai terminal.

Vérification documentaire : huit sources primaires ouvertes ; faits externes
séparés des recommandations ; aucune annonce d'implémentation ; liens entre
AR01 à AR07 conservés. Risques encore à résoudre à l'implémentation : effets
incertains, mélange de scopes, cycles, budgets et attribution trompeuse des
résultats au modèle. Aucun test runtime ni build requis pour ce seul document.

Un worker disponible peut recevoir le prochain travail utile au lieu de mourir
automatiquement. Le contexte déjà acquis compte dans ce choix. Ce contexte doit
néanmoins être rafraîchi s'il est devenu périmé ; le garder chaud ne le rend pas
valide pour tous les travaux.

## 31. Agent assist

Un worker peut demander une aide ciblée en nommant besoin et travail bloqué.
Le helper retourne découverte, preuves, limites, implications et inconnues.
Éviter les longues conversations inter-agents et les chaînes d'aide sans but.
Les résultats utiles rejoignent l'état partagé avec leur provenance.

## 32. Knowledge delta routing

Une découverte entre dans l'état commun ; sa pertinence détermine quels workers
reçoivent le delta. Chaque destinataire voit ce qui affecte son travail, avec
sources et révision. Aucun broadcast intégral des chats ni contournement des
permissions par agrégation.

## 33. Peer / adversarial review

Adapter l'indépendance et l'effort de revue au risque, à l'incertitude et à
l'étendue d'impact. Une vérification indépendante cherche les défauts et les
preuves manquantes. Ne pas lancer systématiquement plusieurs reviewers pour
chaque changement trivial.

## 34. Live steering

Une correction humaine révise immédiatement le contexte partagé. Les workers
non touchés continuent ; les concernés checkpointent et replanifient ; les
travaux invalides s'arrêtent à une frontière sûre. La saisie reste disponible.
Le message n'attend pas derrière une réponse et ne lance pas un travail isolé.

## 35. Sync barrier

Stop, faisons le point peut arrêter les nouvelles prises de travail, atteindre
les checkpoints sûrs, persister et réconcilier, puis présenter le point commun.
La personne peut continuer, rediriger ou annuler. Une barrière de synchronisation
ne signifie pas forcément tuer tous les processus.

## 36. Human legibility

Maintenir la compréhension utile du travail : ce qui est touché, où on en est,
pourquoi, comment on sait, ce qu'on ignore et ce qui change. La vue humaine est
une projection du même état que les agents. Elle ne raconte pas chaque opération
et ne demande pas à l'utilisateur de coordonner le runtime.

## 37. Human delta

Présenter les nouvelles informations qui modifient la compréhension nécessaire.
Exemple : une propriété est aussi consommée par mobile ; sa suppression casse
un contrat ; le plan préserve donc la compatibilité. Associer changement,
implication et décision, avec source accessible. Éviter de répéter tout l'historique.

## 38. Confirmation by exception

Routine : silencieuse. Information : affichée. Hypothèse importante réversible :
affichée avec continuation autorisée. Décision indispensable, irréversible ou
réellement ambiguë : blocage adapté. Ces niveaux ne créent pas de droits et
n'autorisent pas à déduire une approbation du silence.

## 39. Human model

Suivre seulement faits, décisions, hypothèses et questions effectivement
communiqués, avec dernière synchronisation. Comparer ce registre au savoir du
système pour décider d'un delta utile. Présenté, livré et acquitté sont distincts ;
aucun de ces états ne prouve les pensées ou la compréhension de l'humain.
